title: Not in our hands (Avot 4:15)
hookLine: the corner-cutter gets promoted, the careful one gets the bad news: Yannai says we cannot explain it
tomorrow: she beat you. do you say hi first?

lines: IS THERE AN ANSWER FOR WHY?
AVOT, FOR ONCE, DOESN'T GIVE ONE.
cards: Is there an answer for why? The one who cut corners gets the promotion. The one who did everything right gets the bad news.
Sometimes it's small, the wrong show picked, the wrong name called. Sometimes it's the biggest question there is. Pirkei Avot has been handing out answers for weeks: do this, don't do that.
And then Rabbi Yannai steps up, and for once, Avot doesn't give one.

teach.h: A BOOK OF ANSWERS, AND ONE REFUSAL.
teach.b: Here's Rabbi Yannai, in plain words. It is not in our hands, neither the ease of the wicked nor the suffering of the righteous. That's the puzzle.
A book of answers, and here's a saying that refuses to answer. Why keep it? Because the question is older than Avot, and the Bible doesn't hide it.

The prophet Jeremiah asks God out loud: "Wherefore doth the way of the wicked prosper?" Job asks it for chapters. Yannai sits in that line of honest askers, and he says what they found: we can't explain it.

Commentators even read his words two ways. Some hear: we can't explain why it happens. Others hear: we don't have the ease of the wicked, and we may not be spared the suffering of the righteous either.
Either reading, he doesn't make up a reason. He doesn't say the good are secretly being punished, or that the winners secretly lost. He refuses the easy answer that would hurt someone.
And notice what's still in our hands, all around this saying: how we judge, how we greet, how we honor people. Avot doesn't stop acting because one question has no answer.
It holds the question and keeps going.

how: In Jewish mourning and comfort, visitors are taught not to explain a loss to the mourner, and many simply sit with them; the question of why the righteous suffer is studied in Job and argued in the Talmud without one settled answer.

games.q: what does “not in our hands” mean?
o: we can't explain why the wicked thrive or the good suffer
the outcome of a court case belongs to the judges
nothing we do makes any difference to how life goes

games.q: who asked the question — tap the pairs.
p: it is not in our hands
why does the way of the wicked prosper?
how we judge, greet and honor people

s: Jewish tradition says suffering always means a person did something wrong
Yannai refuses to make up a reason; he says we cannot explain the suffering of the righteous.
commentators read Yannai's words in more than one way
we can't explain it, or we're not spared it either: both are offered.
the Bible itself asks why the wicked prosper
Jeremiah asks it of God out loud.

games.q: a friend's dad, the kindest man you know, gets seriously sick. your friend asks you, why him? what fits Rabbi Yannai's saying?
o: say honestly that you don't know why, and stay with your friend.
explain that everything happens for a reason, even if it's hidden.
point out that hard things make people stronger in the end.
games.why: it is not in our hands. Yannai won't invent a reason that could hurt someone. what is in our hands is staying.

practice: Close your eyes, and let one question come up that has no answer for you right now: something unfair, something you can't explain. Don't answer it, and don't push it away.
Just hold it, the way you'd hold a stone in an open hand, for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Not in our hands. Rabbi Yannai: we cannot explain the ease of the wicked or the suffering of the righteous.

orig.note: Hebrew: it is not in our hands, Rabbi Yannai's opening words.

carryVoice: Keep this one: not in our hands, said honestly, without a made-up reason. Thirty-eight of sixty, held.

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 4:15 (Rabbi Yannai: it is not in our hands, neither the tranquility of the wicked nor the suffering of the righteous)
